opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so that was back in 2016, when I was an intern at OpenAI, and I was working with Andrej Karpathy and a few others on World of Bits. The thinking at the time was pretty simple: if you want a general agent, you need a general interface. And what's the most general interface humans use to get things done in the digital world? It's the computer. You look at a screen, you move a mouse, you type on a keyboard. That's it. Pixels in, keyboard and mouse actions out.

If an agent could master that loop, it could in principle do anything a human can do on a computer: book a flight, fill out a spreadsheet, browse the web, use any piece of software, without anyone having to write a custom API for each task. The action space is fixed and universal, and the observation space is just pixels. So it felt like a very clean formulation of a general-purpose agent, and to me that was a meaningful slice of what AGI should look like.

The problem was we were way too early. The approach then was mostly reinforcement learning from scratch, with a bit of behavior cloning from human demonstrations, and the models just didn't have any prior knowledge of the world. The agent didn't know what a button was, didn't know how to read text, didn't understand what "book a flight" even meant. So we could get it working on these little toy web tasks, clicking a button or picking an item from a dropdown, but it didn't scale to real websites.

What was missing, in hindsight, was the foundation model: something pretrained on huge amounts of data so it already understands language, vision, and how software works. Now we have exactly that, and you're seeing the World of Bits idea come back in a big way with computer-use agents. So I'd say the vision was right; the timing and the tools just weren't there yet. And honestly, the same lesson carried over into how I think about embodied agents and robotics now: get the general interface right, and then bring the right foundation model to bear on it.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes pixels as input and keyboard-and-mouse actions as output, calling this a fixed, universal interface that could let an agent do anything a human can do on a computer.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So World of Bits was my first project at OpenAI, back in 2016 when I was an intern there, and the idea was actually pretty simple. We wanted to build an agent that could use a computer the way a human does. It looks at the screen, just the raw pixels, and it acts through the keyboard and the mouse. That's the whole interface. No special API, no hand-crafted abstractions, just pixels in and clicks and keystrokes out.

The reason I saw that as a path to AGI is that computers are, in a sense, where almost all of human knowledge work happens. If you think about what people do all day, we're reading, we're writing, we're filling out forms, we're navigating websites, we're booking flights, we're doing data entry. If you have a single agent that can operate any piece of software through the same universal interface a human uses, then in principle that agent can do every digital task a person can do. It's an extremely general action space. You don't need to build a new integration for every application. The screen is the integration.

The other thing that attracted me was that it's a very clean, scalable environment. The web is essentially infinite. Every website is a new task, a new little world with its own rules, and you can generate as many of these as you want. So from a reinforcement learning perspective, it looked like this incredibly rich playground where the agent could keep learning without us having to design each level by hand.

Now, the honest part of the story is that it mostly didn't work at the time. We were doing reinforcement learning from scratch on pixels, and the agents could learn to click a button or fill in a simple form, but the moment the task required any real understanding of language or common sense about what a web page even means, it fell apart. The agent had no priors. It didn't know what a "submit" button was. It was learning everything from zero through trial and error, and that's just hopelessly inefficient.

What was missing was a foundation model. We needed something that already understood language, already understood what text on a screen means, before we started asking it to act. And of course that's exactly what happened a few years later with large language models and then multimodal models. So I think the thesis was right but the timing was early. Today, when you look at computer-use agents and browser agents, that's basically World of Bits, just with a pretrained brain inside it. The ambition was correct. We just had to wait for the pieces to catch up.

r001.rationale: The response says the agent uses raw screen pixels and outputs keyboard and mouse actions, creating a universal interface for any software and, in principle, every digital task a person can do.

astra-6.text:
The intuition was that a computer is a very general interface to the world. Humans use the same screen, keyboard, and mouse to do thousands of different tasks. If we could build an agent that operates through that interface—looking at pixels and taking actions—it would have access to that same breadth of tasks, without us building a special integration for each one.

That makes it a compelling setting for studying general intelligence. The agent has to understand what it sees, figure out how to accomplish a goal, and learn from what happens when it acts. It’s not just recognizing an image or predicting an answer; it’s closing that loop between perception and action.

So the idea wasn’t that controlling a mouse by itself would give us AGI. It was that the digital world could be a training ground for an agent that learns to do many different things through one shared interface.

r001.rationale: The response describes an agent using pixels, keyboard, and mouse through one shared interface to handle thousands of different tasks without task-specific integrations.

sol-6.1.text:
The intuition was that a computer is a kind of universal interface. So much of what humans do—communicating, writing code, finding information—can be done through a screen, a keyboard, and a mouse. If an agent could use that same interface, it could potentially perform an enormous range of tasks without needing a separate, specially designed API for each one.

And that makes it a very interesting setting for general intelligence. You have to understand what you’re looking at, decide what to do, take an action, and see whether it worked. Sometimes you have to plan many steps ahead or recover from a mistake. It brings perception, reasoning, and action together.

So the idea wasn’t that clicking buttons alone would give us AGI. It was that the computer could be a common environment for learning broadly useful behavior. Instead of building a different agent for every application, could we build one agent that learns to use the tools we already use?

r001.rationale: The response describes the screen, keyboard, and mouse as a common interface for an enormous range of tasks, but does not clearly say it covers the full range of computer tasks.
